sections.authorBiography: Francis Scott Key Fitzgerald was born in St. Paul, Minnesota, on 24 September 1896, named for a distant relative who wrote "The Star-Spangled Banner." He attended Princeton University but left without a degree and joined the U.S. Army in 1917; the war ended before he was sent overseas. While stationed near Montgomery, Alabama, he met Zelda Sayre, who married him in 1920, a week after his first novel, This Side of Paradise, made him famous. The Fitzgeralds became celebrities of what he named "the Jazz Age," living in New York, on Long Island (Great Neck, 1922–24) and in France, where he wrote most of The Great Gatsby. His later years were marked by debt, alcoholism and Zelda's psychiatric illness; he published Tender Is the Night (1934), wrote for Hollywood, and died of a heart attack in Hollywood on 21 December 1940, aged 44, leaving The Last Tycoon unfinished. He believed himself a failure; Gatsby's reputation grew only after his death.
sections.historicalContext: The novel is set in the summer of 1922 on Long Island and in New York City. Fitzgerald wrote most of it in France in 1924, after living in Great Neck, Long Island, which became his West Egg. The 1920s brought Prohibition (the Eighteenth Amendment, in force from 1920), which made bootlegging and organized crime enormously profitable; a booming stock market and new fortunes; mass-produced cars; jazz; and new freedoms for young women (the "flapper"). Meyer Wolfshiem's fixing of the 1919 World Series alludes to the real Black Sox scandal, usually linked to the gambler Arnold Rothstein. Tom Buchanan's talk of a book about "the Coloured Empires" echoes real racist best-sellers of the period, such as Lothrop Stoddard's The Rising Tide of Color (1920).

publicationAndReception.publication: Charles Scribner's Sons published The Great Gatsby on 10 April 1925, edited by Maxwell Perkins, with Francis Cugat's painting of a woman's face above a carnival-lit city on the jacket. Fitzgerald had considered other titles, including "Trimalchio in West Egg." The book entered the United States public domain on 1 January 2021.
publicationAndReception.then: Sales disappointed Fitzgerald: the book sold far fewer copies than his first two novels, and some reviews were dismissive. Writers admired it; T. S. Eliot wrote to Fitzgerald that it seemed "the first step that American fiction has taken since Henry James." When Fitzgerald died in 1940 he thought himself forgotten.
publicationAndReception.now: Interest revived after his death; during the Second World War the book was printed in the Armed Services Editions sent to American troops. It is now one of the most taught American novels and a standard candidate for "the Great American Novel." Film versions include those of 1949, 1974 (with Robert Redford) and 2013 (Baz Luhrmann). Modern readers debate Nick's reliability, the novel's treatment of class and race, and what it says about the American Dream.

sections.overview: In the summer of 1922 Nick Carraway, a young Midwesterner, rents a small house on Long Island next to the mansion of the mysterious Jay Gatsby, who throws enormous parties. Across the bay live Nick's cousin Daisy and her rich husband Tom. Nick tells us what he learned that summer about Gatsby and the people around him.

mainThemes.note: Gatsby remakes himself from nothing; ask whether the dream is noble, corrupt or impossible.
old money, new money and the people who pay for both.
"Can't repeat the past? Why of course you can!"
Gatsby's invented self, Daisy as a dream, Nick's own self-image as honest.
who cleans up after the careless rich?

sections.whyItMatters: The Great Gatsby gives American culture a vocabulary for ambition, reinvention and excess, and asks whether wealth can buy belonging or happiness. Students practice reading a narrator critically, tracing symbols that change meaning, and connecting a 1925 novel to questions about class, race, gender and the American Dream today.

spoilerOverview.text: Gatsby, born James Gatz, loved Daisy before the war and has made a fortune, partly through bootlegging, to win her back. Nick arranges their reunion; the affair revives. In a hot confrontation at the Plaza Hotel, Tom exposes Gatsby's criminal dealings and Daisy cannot say she never loved Tom. Driving Gatsby's car home, Daisy hits and kills Tom's mistress, Myrtle Wilson; Gatsby takes the blame. Tom tells Myrtle's grieving husband George that the car was Gatsby's; Wilson shoots Gatsby and then himself. Tom and Daisy leave town; almost no one comes to Gatsby's funeral. Nick returns to the Midwest.

segments.phase: I do: the book in one passage
segments.activity: Model a close reading of one passage using the written think-aloud below.
segments.script: First, meaning. I read “So we beat on, boats against the current, borne back ceaselessly into the past” slowly and put it in my own words: Nick says we keep rowing forward like boats against the current, but we are carried back again and again into the past. Next, craft. I notice the image of boats rowing against a current, and the "b" sounds (beat, boats, borne, back) that make the sentence pull like a tide. The strongest word is “ceaselessly”: it means without stopping, so the struggle against the past never ends. Then, effect. What does the novel's last sentence say about Gatsby's dream and about us? My answer: Gatsby's effort to recover 1917 and Daisy is everyone's effort; Fitzgerald ends by saying that striving toward the future keeps dragging us back to what we have lost.

segments.activity: Exit ticket on the author and context (answer given).
segments.script: Fitzgerald wrote the novel in 1924 during the boom years after World War I, and he and Zelda lived the glamorous, hard-drinking life of the Jazz Age. How might that experience shape a novel about wealthy parties? Answer: Accept answers such as: he knew the excitement and emptiness of rich parties; he felt like an outsider among old money; Prohibition-era bootlegging was all around him.

strategies.label: Wait time
strategies.howTo: Pause at least 3 seconds after asking (5 to 10 for DOK 3 and 4 questions) before calling on anyone, and pause again after a student answers so others can add on. Call on students at random, not only volunteers.

strategies.label: Think-pair-share
strategies.howTo: One minute of silent thinking or jotting, two minutes with a partner, then pairs report. Use it for every DOK 3 and 4 question so all students rehearse an answer.

strategies.label: Follow-up probes
strategies.howTo: Answer a response with a probe instead of a verdict: ask for the line that proves it, ask "why?" or "how do you know?", or ask another student to agree, extend or challenge.

strategies.label: Student-generated questions
strategies.howTo: Students write their own questions at each level (a recall, a "why/how" and a "should/what if" question), trade them, and answer a classmate's. The teacher picks one or two for the whole class.

strategies.label: Turn and talk
strategies.howTo: A 60-second partner check for literal questions, so every student says the answer aloud before one is called on.

strategies.label: Cold call with support
strategies.howTo: Call on a student by name after the wait time; if they are stuck, offer a choice of two answers or let them "phone a friend" and come back to them.

strategies.label: Socratic circle
strategies.howTo: Inner circle discusses for 5 minutes while the outer circle tracks evidence and questions; then swap.

strategies.label: Four corners / take a stand
strategies.howTo: Students move to Agree / Somewhat agree / Somewhat disagree / Disagree and must cite a line to defend the position; anyone may move after hearing evidence.

literal.label: Literal / recall
literal.scaffold: Sentence starter: “In this chapter, … because the text says …”
literal.extension: Note how this detail is set up or echoed elsewhere in The Great Gatsby.
followUps: Where exactly does it say that? Read us the line.
Who can add a detail that comes just before or after?

inferential.label: Inferential / analytical
inferential.scaffold: Sentence starter: “The text says …, which suggests … because …”
inferential.extension: Test your reading against one critical approach (formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist) and say what it adds.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?

evaluative.label: Evaluative / synthesis / creative
evaluative.scaffold: Sentence starter: “I (dis)agree that … because …; someone might object that …, but …”
evaluative.extension: Situate your judgment in a critical conversation about The Great Gatsby: whose reading does yours support or challenge?
followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?

middleSchool.note: Excerpt-based: read the passage aloud first; use the scaffolds; accept partial answers and build with probes.

hsFreshman.note: Use the scaffolds for literal and inferential items; require one quotation for every inferential answer.

hsSophomore.note: Require a quotation and an explanation; push evaluative answers to address a counterclaim.

hsJunior.note: Emphasize structure and ambiguity; students should name where the text leaves matters open.

hsSenior.note: Weigh competing interpretations; students should defend the stronger reading.

ap.note: Treat each evaluative item as a thesis rehearsal: defensible claim, purposeful evidence, commentary on choices.

collegeFreshman.note: Add the extension: connect answers to historical context and one secondary perspective.

collegeSophomore.note: Use the extensions: genre and period conventions, and a published critic.

collegeJunior.note: Use the extensions: name a critical method and test it against the passage.

collegeSenior.note: Use the extensions: connect the chapter to the whole work and the scholarship.

graduate.note: Use the extensions: position answers in a critical conversation and the textual history.

questioning.alignment: Questioning design (our description; see docs/questioning-alignment.md): every lesson offers questions at three cognitive levels with DOK tags, built-in wait time, follow-up probes after each answer, think-pair-share for higher-order items and a student-generated question routine, with a level-specific focus set for each of the eleven rigor levels. It is designed to support classroom observation frameworks such as the NIET Teaching Standards Rubric (Questioning indicator); it is not NIET material and is not endorsed by NIET.

segments.activity: Students write to the bell-ringer, then pair-share.
segments.script: Project the day's bell-ringer question (each lesson of The Great Gatsby has its own). Students write silently for 5 minutes, then pair-share for 3. Call on one volunteer and one non-volunteer, and connect their answers to the American Dream.

segments.activity: The day's key words in context, with verified word histories.
segments.script: Introduce the day's words in the sentences where they appear in The Great Gatsby. Read each sentence aloud, ask students to guess the meaning from context, then give the gloss and the word history. Students copy one word into their journal with their own sentence.

Give the 10-minute background talk from the day's lesson: what happens in this chapter, the context a reader needs, and the literary elements to watch. Pause once to ask a check-for-understanding question.

segments.activity: Model the close reading of the anchor quotation using the written think-aloud in the day's lesson.
segments.script: Read the anchor passage aloud twice. Model the three steps out loud: what the words say, what craft choice stands out and why, and what effect it has on the reader. The day's lesson gives the passage and a full written think-aloud.

segments.activity: Guided analysis of a second quotation; expected answers given.
segments.script: Display the second passage. Students annotate it in pairs using the same three steps; circulate, then take answers to the two guided questions and confirm them against the expected answers in the day's lesson.

segments.activity: Independent annotation and a claim-evidence-reasoning paragraph (exemplar given).
segments.script: Students annotate the chapter on their own (three marks with a margin note each) and write one claim-evidence-reasoning paragraph on the day's focus, then begin the writing prompt at their assigned rigor level.

segments.activity: Structured discussion from the 30 tiered questions, with facilitation notes.
segments.script: Run a 10-minute discussion from the day's anchor question and tiered questions. Start with literal checks, move to inference, and end with one evaluative question that ties the chapter to the American Dream.

segments.activity: Chapter quiz in the app and an exit ticket (answer given).
segments.script: Students take the chapter quiz in the app, then answer the one-sentence exit ticket with a short quotation. Collect the tickets to plan the next lesson.

segments.activity: Summarize the lesson and preview the next reading.
segments.script: Restate the day's takeaway in one sentence, ask two students to name the line that best proves it, and preview the next reading in The Great Gatsby.

objectives: Students will cite at least 2 quotations, with locations, to support each written claim about what the text says explicitly and implicitly (scored on the writing-prompt rubric).
Students will trace one theme across at least 3 sections of the novel in the final paper, earning at least 70 of 100 rubric points.
Students will explain how characters, setting and point of view interact in at least 3 exit tickets, each meeting the claim-evidence-reasoning criteria.
Students will determine the in-context meaning of taught vocabulary, scoring at least 80% on the vocabulary items of the chapter quizzes.
Students will write an argument with a clear claim, reasons and relevant evidence, scoring at least 80% on the unit test's short-answer scoring guides.

The words “valley” and “ashes” carry that meaning: they are the charged choices in the line, and changing either would soften the effect. Fitzgerald calls it "a valley of ashes" watched by the eyes of Doctor T. J. Eckleburg, and Tom's casual violence there ("broke her nose with his open hand") shows how the rich treat those below them.

Earlier, in Chapter II, paragraph 1, the text reads “This is a valley of ashes”, which shows the wasteland that wealth leaves behind. In Chapter III, “In his blue gardens men and girls came and went like moths among the whisperings and the champagne and the stars” (Chapter III, paragraph 1), which shows the party as a dream, guests as moths to a light. The owl-eyed man is amazed that Gatsby's books are real; the man himself is the illusion.

The dream shrinks when reached. The evidence is “the colossal significance of that light had now vanished forever” (Chapter V, paragraph 121). This develops illusion and reality: no real woman can match "the colossal vitality of his illusion.". The words “significance” and “vanished” carry that meaning: they are the charged choices in the line, and changing either would soften the effect. Nick notes that "the colossal significance of that light had now vanished forever" and that "Daisy tumbled short of his dreams," while Daisy weeps over "such beautiful shirts.".

Self-invention. The evidence is “sprang from his Platonic conception of himself” (Chapter VI, paragraph 7). This develops the past and time: Gatsby insists he can repeat the past. The words “conception” and “himself” carry that meaning: they are the charged choices in the line, and changing either would soften the effect. Nick reveals "James Gatz—that was really, or at least legally, his name" and that Gatsby "sprang from his Platonic conception of himself," which explains his answer to Nick's "You can't repeat the past": "Why of course you can!".

Gatsby's insight about Daisy. The evidence is “Her voice is full of money” (Chapter VII, paragraph 104). This develops class and money: old money defeats new money. The words “money” and “voice” carry that meaning: they are the charged choices in the line, and changing either would soften the effect. Gatsby recognizes "Her voice is full of money," and Daisy's "I did love him once—but I loved you too" destroys his demand for total possession of the past.

Daisy's answer. The evidence is “I did love him once—but I loved you too” (Chapter VII, paragraph 263). This develops class and money: old money defeats new money. The words “loved” and “once” carry that meaning: they are the charged choices in the line, and changing either would soften the effect. Gatsby recognizes "Her voice is full of money," and Daisy's "I did love him once—but I loved you too" destroys his demand for total possession of the past.

Nick's verdict. The evidence is “They’re a rotten crowd” (Chapter VIII, paragraph 45). This develops the American Dream: Gatsby dies still believing. The words “rotten” and “crowd” carry that meaning: they are the charged choices in the line, and changing either would soften the effect. He shouts "They're a rotten crowd" and "You're worth the whole damn bunch put together," while Wilson insists "God sees everything" to the billboard eyes.

The Dutch sailors' first sight of America: the original dream. The evidence is “a fresh, green breast of the new world” (Chapter IX, paragraph 159). This develops carelessness and morality: Tom and Daisy are careless people. The words “breast” and “world” carry that meaning: they are the charged choices in the line, and changing either would soften the effect. Nick condemns the "careless people, Tom and Daisy" who "retreated back into their money," but says "Gatsby believed in the green light, the orgiastic future that year by year recedes before us," and ends with "boats against the current, borne back ceaselessly into the past.".

Nick's verdict. The evidence is “They were careless people, Tom and Daisy—they smashed up things and creatures and then retreated back into their money” (Chapter IX, paragraph 154). This develops carelessness and morality: Tom and Daisy are careless people. The words “creatures” and “retreated” carry that meaning: they are the charged choices in the line, and changing either would soften the effect. Nick condemns the "careless people, Tom and Daisy" who "retreated back into their money," but says "Gatsby believed in the green light, the orgiastic future that year by year recedes before us," and ends with "boats against the current, borne back ceaselessly into the past.".

finalPaper.title: The Great Gatsby: final paper (formal literary analysis)

prompts.text: Analyze how F. Scott Fitzgerald develops the American Dream across The Great Gatsby. Trace the idea through at least three moments (beginning, middle and end) and argue what the ending finally suggests.
Choose one recurring symbol, image or motif in The Great Gatsby and argue how its meaning changes over the novel and why that change matters to class and money.
Analyze a central character's choices in The Great Gatsby. Argue whether the novel judges that character, and how its structure or point of view shapes your answer.
Two readers disagree about whether The Great Gatsby finally endorses or criticizes its society's view of the past and time. Weigh both readings and argue for one, answering the strongest objection.

evidence.sections: at least three sections, from the beginning, middle and end

rubric.descriptor: A specific, arguable claim that answers the prompt and organizes the paper.
Well-chosen, accurately quoted and cited passages from across the work, meeting the evidence requirement.
Explains how language, structure and literary elements create meaning; goes beyond summary.
Logical progression, clear topic sentences and transitions; introduction and conclusion frame the argument.
Formal academic voice, present tense for literature, correct grammar and MLA format.

Thesis: Specific, arguable and precise; it organizes every section.
Clear and arguable, but broad in places.
States a topic or a summary more than an argument.
Evidence: Accurate, well-chosen quotations from across the work, all cited; meets the requirement.
Accurate and cited, but clustered in one part of the work.
Too few quotations, or some inaccurate or uncited.
Analysis: Explains how specific words, structure and devices create meaning; weighs a competing reading.
Explains the evidence, with some close reading.
Mostly summary; the link to the claim is asserted, not shown.
Organization: Each paragraph advances the argument; transitions show logic.
Order is loose; paragraphs repeat or drift.
Style and conventions: Formal, precise, present tense; MLA format; virtually error-free.
Formal with a few errors that do not obscure meaning.
Informal or error-prone in ways that distract.

finalPaper.exemplar: The first chapter sets up Nick as a narrator whose claims of fairness must be tested. The text makes this visible when it says “a single green light, minute and far away, that might have been the end of a dock” (Chapter I, paragraph 152). He opens with his father's advice he has been "turning over in my mind ever since" and claims to reserve judgment, yet his portraits of Tom and Daisy are sharply judgmental, and he alone sees Gatsby reach toward "a single green light, minute and far away.". A full paper would carry this reading through the beginning, middle and end, and answer the strongest competing reading.

criticalVoices.quote: The thing that chiefly interests the basic Fitzgerald is still the florid show of modern American life—and especially the devil’s dance that goes on at the top.
criticalVoices.speaker: H. L. Mencken, critic and journalist
criticalVoices.source: Review of The Great Gatsby, Chicago Sunday Tribune (3 May 1925), reprinted as "Time Machine" (10 Oct 2014), middle paragraphs
criticalVoices.useNote: Thesis frame: if the novel's subject is "the devil's dance … at the top," is the American Dream its target or its victim? Test with Chapter III (the party) and the final page.
criticalVoices.linkedObjective: Final paper Prompts 1 and 2: the American Dream, class and money.

criticalVoices.speaker: Edwin Clark, reviewer
criticalVoices.source: "Scott Fitzgerald Looks Into Middle Age," The New York Times Book Review (19 April 1925), review text
